name: bic
why: A C interpreter that doubles as an API explorer, letting you poke at libraries interactively, which is a genuinely useful strange idea.

brief.what_it_is: bic is a C interpreter and API explorer. You type C statements into a REPL prompt (BIC>), and #include system headers so you can call real library functions such as fopen and fputs directly, with no wrapping main() needed. It can also run a whole C file with -s file.c, calling its main(). After each expression it prints the result, and the ?name inspector prints type and variable details such as size and declaration location.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it exists to let developers explore and test C APIs using a read eval print loop, also known as a REPL.
brief.how_it_works: The lexer and parser are generated from parser.m4 and lex.m4, producing two bison parsers and two flex lexers, one grammar for REPL input and one for C files. Parsed programs become generic tree objects defined in a lisp-like c.lang file, and the evaluator walks that tree recursively. Calls to external functions are marshalled into registers per the calling convention and branched to, with separate x86_64 and aarch64 code.

brief.install_notes: Build dependencies: Flex, GNU Bison, GNU Automake, GNU M4, GNU Autoconf Archive, plus libtool and pkg-config in the Debian list. Runtime dependencies are GNU Readline and GNU MP (libgmp). The README gives apt-get and brew package lists, the autoreconf/configure/make/make install sequence, and a Docker route and an AUR package. No accounts are needed. On first launch, bic reads ~/.bic if present and evaluates it as startup code, which is useful for defining functions you use often.
brief.standout: Most C REPLs hand you a language sandbox. This one lets you #include real system headers and call into the actual libc or other shared libraries, and the ?name inspector reports declarations and sizes. The README also describes a -l option for loading other libraries such as Capstone, though the example is not shown in the text I read.

brief.caveats: Only x86_64 and aarch64 are supported, because the external-call code is written per architecture. It is GPL-2.0. Building needs a toolchain of flex, bison, automake, m4 and autoconf-archive, and macOS needs the YACC override shown above. The README's Capstone example has its command missing from the text, so the -l usage is not fully documented there. Bare statements are only allowed in the REPL, not in C files. The ?name inspector is REPL-only.

entry.title: bic
entry.tldr: A C interpreter with a REPL prompt that lets you #include real system headers and call actual libc functions, no main() required.
entry.deeper_look:
bic gives C a read-eval-print loop. You get a `BIC>` prompt, type C statements, and see the result of each expression printed back. You can `#include` system headers and call real library functions such as `fopen` and `fputs` straight away, without wrapping anything in `main()`. It can also run a whole file with `-s file.c`, which calls that file's `main()`.

The README says it exists to let developers explore and test C APIs with a REPL. Most C REPLs give you a sandboxed language. bic reaches into the real shared libraries on your machine. A `?name` inspector in the REPL prints type and variable details, such as size and where something was declared. The README also describes a `-l` option for loading other libraries such as Capstone, though the example is missing from the text.

Under the hood, bison and flex generate two parsers, one for REPL input and one for C files. Programs become generic tree objects defined in a lisp-like `c.lang` file, and the evaluator walks that tree recursively. To call external functions, bic marshals arguments into registers following the calling convention and branches to the function. That code is written separately for x86_64 and aarch64, which is the door into ABIs and how a call actually happens.

On first launch bic reads `~/.bic` if it exists and evaluates it as startup code, which is handy for defining functions you use often.
entry.install:
brew install bic
# runtime needs GNU Readline and GMP (gmp is pulled in as a dependency); only x86_64 and aarch64 are supported

Evaluates test.c by calling its main(); the README's example prints "Factorial of 4 is: 24".

entry.whats_unique: Most C REPLs hand you a language sandbox. bic lets you include real system headers and call into the actual libc or other shared libraries, and it can report declarations and sizes with `?name`.
entry.caveats: Only x86_64 and aarch64 are supported because external calls are written per architecture, and the brief could not confirm recent commit activity.
